subject: Hierarchical logistic regression optimization and questions

messages.author: 5a8bfcb87fd22c3b
messages.subject: Hierarchical logistic regression optimization and questions
parts:
Hello,

I've been working on a hierarchical logistic model and while I've been able to make it work, I have some questions about Stan that perhaps someone here will be able to answer.

The model code is:

data {
    int<lower = 0> n_subject1;
    int<lower = 0> n_trials;
    int<lower = 0> n_subject2;
    int<lower = 0, upper = n_subject1 - 1> subject1[n_trials];
    int<lower = 0, upper=1> trials[n_trials];
    int<lower = 0, upper = n_subject2 - 1> subject2[n_trials];
}
parameters {
    vector[n_subject1] raw_subject1_effects;
    vector[n_subject2] raw_subject2_effects;

    real intercept;
    real<lower = 0> sigma_subject1;
    real<lower = 0> sigma_subject2;
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[n_subject1] subject1_effects;
    vector[n_subject2] subject2_effects;

    subject1_effects <- raw_subject1_effects - mean(raw_subject1_effects);
    subject2_effects <- raw_subject2_effects - mean(raw_subject2_effects);
}
model {
    vector[n_trials] alpha;

    intercept ~ normal(0, 10000);
    sigma_subject1 ~ uniform(0, 100);
    sigma_subject2 ~ uniform(0, 100);

    raw_subject1_effects ~ normal(0, sigma_subject1);
    raw_subject2_effects ~ normal(0, sigma_subject2);

    for (i in 1:n_trials)
        alpha[i] <- intercept + subject1_effects[subject1[i] + 1] + subject2_effects[subject2[i] + 1];

    trials ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha);
}


The model is fairly standard and I've added sum to zero constraints on the random effects for the two different types of subjects.

First of all, is there any way to make my model more efficient? It samples fairly quickly but I'd like any pointers as I'm new to using Stan.

Second, as I was trying to speed up my model, I was monitoring how much memory each chain consumed and how quickly they finished. Using a 10,000 item subset of the full dataset with the model above with 4 chains and 5000 samples, it finished after about 2 minutes and each process used about 250 MB of memory.

However, at one point I tried moving the declaration and computation of alpha into the transformed parameters block rather than the model block. It took finishing time to about 20 minutes and memory usage per process to about 1.2GB per process. Why did it do this? What's the difference between declaring and computing alpha in the model block as opposed to the transformed parameters block and why did it cause such a difference in performance?

Lastly, if I remove the wide prior on the intercept, this also causes the model to sample slower by roughly one order of magnitude. Is this because if I don't, it assumes a uniform distribution over the real numbers and thus has a much wider space to explore in sampling? This is just a guess, I'd love for someone to correct me or confirm my suspicion.

Thanks,
Rick

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical logistic regression optimization and questions
parts:
Hi Rick,

Which interface to Stan are you using? RStan? Some more comments below.

Jonah

However, at one point I tried moving the declaration and computation of alpha into the transformed parameters block rather than the model block. It took finishing time to about 20 minutes and memory usage per process to about 1.2GB per process. Why did it do this? What's the difference between declaring and computing alpha in the model block as opposed to the transformed parameters block and why did it cause such a difference in performance?
If you declare something in transformed parameters then it's values will be stored whereas the model block is discarded from memory.

Lastly, if I remove the wide prior on the intercept, this also causes the model to sample slower by roughly one order of magnitude. Is this because if I don't, it assumes a uniform distribution over the real numbers and thus has a much wider space to explore in sampling? This is just a guess, I'd love for someone to correct me or confirm my suspicion.

Yeah that's right. The default prior is a (potentially improper) uniform on the support of the parameter. 

In general we recommend informative or weakly informative priors, rather than the wide priors you currently have. For logistic regression with scaled predictors the coefficients are basically guaranteed to be small (in the -5 to 5 range, roughly), so even something like a normal(0,5) is not a very informative prior. I think Aki recommends a t distribution with 7 df as a default prior for logistic regression coefficients. Of course if you have real prior knowledge you can do even better. 

Also for the scale parameters (your sigmas) the constrained uniform can be problematic. We'd recommend a 'soft' constraint via some decaying distribution, like cauchy(0, 2.5) or even tighter, with the parameter declared with lower=0. If you do want to use the uniforms then you should declare sigma with the upper bound you want and then not specify a prior in the model block for it.

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical logistic regression optimization and questions
parts:
Hey Jonah,

Thanks a ton for the information! I also should have specified that I'm calling Stan through Pystan and not Rstan. Does that make a difference in terms of efficiency?

Regarding the choice of extremely wide priors, you're right and I adjusted them to weakly informative. That massively sped up sampling - I had only chosen them to be that wide arbitrarily and because I was originally adapting the examples from the PyMC3 site. I'm not sure why they chose such broad priors, but going through the Stan reference manual, they do repeatedly suggest informative or weakly informative priors.

Thanks for the tip on using the cauchy instead of the constrained uniform - I didn't realize that was problematic.

This is a lot clearer now and I've been able to keep my memory usage to a reasonable amount now that I know what causes variables to be stored and what doesn't!

Thanks again,
Rick

On Wednesday, December 16, 2015, <ricka...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hey Jonah,

Thanks a ton for the information! I also should have specified that I'm calling Stan through Pystan and not Rstan. Does that make a difference in terms of efficiency?
Not really, as far as I know. Certainly not enough to warrant switching. They're both good.

Regarding the choice of extremely wide priors, you're right and I adjusted them to weakly informative. That massively sped up sampling - I had only chosen them to be that wide arbitrarily and because I was originally adapting the examples from the PyMC3 site. I'm not sure why they chose such broad priors, but going through the Stan reference manual, they do repeatedly suggest informative or weakly informative priors.

Yeah, those really wide priors used to be the state of the art, and they are still pretty common. But they're rarely the best choice, both for efficiency and for representing prior knowledge (even without much to go on we almost always have strong reasons to believe these parameters will be small if the data are reasonably scaled).

Best,

Jonah
